qs.sol:
ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) is one of the main protocols of the Internet protocol suite.
 It is used by network devices such as routers and gateways to send error messages and operational information—for example, when a requested service is unavailable or a host/router cannot be reached.
 All statements (a), (b), and (c) correctly describe ICMP.

qs.stem: A LAN contains 20 nodes, connected to a central hub (the hub itself is not one of the 20 nodes) in a star topology. If the same 20 nodes are reconfigured into a fully connected mesh network, the number of additional physical links required is :
qs.sol:
A full mesh among 20 nodes needs 20×19/2=190 undirected physical links.

Interpreting 'reconfigured' as repurposing the 20 existing star cables by moving their hub ends to nodes, the number of additional cables to supply is 190−20=170.

topics.deep:
- **Network** = interconnected autonomous nodes sharing resources. **Protocol** = rules of communication: **syntax** (format), **semantics** (meaning), **timing** (when/how fast). Standards bodies: **ISO/OSI, IEEE (802.x), IETF (RFCs), ITU-T**.
- **Topologies:** **Bus** (one shared backbone cable, *multipoint*, terminators at ends, cable break kills all, collisions), **Star** (hub/switch centre; easy fault isolation; centre = single point of failure; most common in LANs), **Ring** (each node has exactly 2 neighbours; token passing; unidirectional or dual ring in FDDI), **Mesh** (point-to-point to every node), **Tree** (hierarchical star-of-stars), **Hybrid** (mix). 'Singleton', 'Car', 'Circle-bus' are fake distractors.
- **Mesh formulae:** links = **n(n−1)/2**; ports (NICs) per node = **n−1**; total ports = n(n−1). Example: 6 nodes -> 15 links, 5 ports each. Bus/ring/star links: bus 1 backbone (n drop lines), ring n, star n.
- **Point-to-point** = dedicated link between two devices; **multipoint (multidrop)** = link shared by >2 devices (bus; also ring is not called multipoint, mesh and star are point-to-point).
- **Network types by size:** **PAN** (~1–10 m, Bluetooth) < **LAN** (building/campus, private, high speed, Ethernet/Wi-Fi) < **MAN** (city; connects LANs; DQDB, FDDI, cable TV network) < **WAN** (country/world; leased lines, satellite, microwave, Internet is the biggest). **CAN** = campus, **SAN** = storage area network, **VPN** = virtual private network over public Internet.
- **LAN technologies:** Ethernet (802.3), Token Ring (802.5), Token Bus (802.4), FDDI (fibre, dual ring, 100 Mbps), Wi-Fi (802.11). **Frame Relay, X.25, ATM, ISDN, leased line, MPLS** are **WAN** technologies. Satellite/microwave/leased links are WAN features, not LAN.
- **Client-server:** dedicated server provides service, central control, scalable, server failure hurts. **Peer-to-peer (P2P):** every node is both client and server, no central server, cheap, poor security/central admin, can scale in capacity (BitTorrent), good for small networks. Any peer can request and serve.
- **Distributed systems:** many autonomous computers connected by a network, appear as a **single coherent system** (transparency). Features: resource sharing, concurrency, scalability (they DO allow scaling), fault tolerance, no shared clock/memory. Types of transparency: access, location, migration, replication, concurrency, failure. **Middleware** sits between OS and applications. Distributed computing aims to make network work like one computer; **parallel computing** has shared memory/tightly coupled.
- **History:** **ARPANET** = Advanced Research Projects Agency Network (US DoD, 1969, packet switching, forerunner of the Internet); switched to TCP/IP on 1 Jan 1983; first message 'LO'. **NSFNET** followed (1986). WWW by Tim Berners-Lee (1989–91, CERN). **Internet** = network of networks using TCP/IP; **Intranet** = private network using Internet tech; **Extranet** = intranet extended to partners.
- **Network classification by transmission:** broadcast (one channel shared, e.g., LAN/radio) vs point-to-point (switched, WAN). **Unicast, multicast, broadcast, anycast** are addressing modes.
- **Comparison table:**
| Topology | Cable/links | Fault effect | Key trap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bus | one backbone | break kills network | multipoint, terminators |
| Star | n links | centre failure kills all | one node failure harmless |
| Ring | n links | one break kills simple ring | token passing |
| Mesh | n(n−1)/2 | very robust | costly, n−1 ports |
- **Common traps:** (1) n(n−1) is wrong for mesh links (counts each twice, valid for *duplex* links on simplex-only setup). (2) Failure of one terminal in a star does not affect others; failure of the central device does. (3) MAN is a collection of LANs but covers a city; WAN is not owned by one org. (4) P2P is not 'less scalable than client-server by definition'.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) number of cables/ports for a full mesh of 10 nodes; (2) which topology uses a backbone with terminators; (3) which is a WAN technology (X.25, Frame Relay, ATM) vs LAN; (4) FDDI topology and speed; (5) differences between Internet, Intranet, Extranet; (6) which of PAN/LAN/MAN/WAN has largest coverage; (7) which topology uses token passing; (8) advantages of client-server vs P2P; (9) transparency types in distributed systems; (10) a hybrid topology made from star and bus.

topics.title: 2. Transmission Modes & Switching Techniques
topics.theory:
- **Simplex**: one direction only (keyboard→CPU, CPU→monitor, TV/radio broadcast).
- **Half-duplex**: both directions, **one at a time** (walkie-talkie, hub-based Ethernet, Wi-Fi).
- **Full-duplex / duplex**: both directions simultaneously (telephone, switched Ethernet, TCP). Only 3 modes exist — **"half simplex" does not exist.**
- Direction terms: unidirectional / bidirectional (half duplex is *not* "multidirectional").
- **Point-to-point** = dedicated link between exactly two devices; **multipoint** = link shared by many (bus).
- **Circuit switching**: dedicated end-to-end path reserved at setup for the whole session; 3 phases setup → transfer → teardown; resources *must* be reserved at setup; used by classic telephone.
- **Packet switching**: message broken into packets, each routed independently (datagram) or along a virtual circuit; links are shared; used by ARPANET/Internet.
- **Message switching**: whole message store-and-forward, no size limit on units.

qs.stem: Communication over walkie-talkie is an example of which of the following modes of communication?
qs.sol: In half-duplex communication, data can flow in both directions, but only one direction at a time. A walkie-talkie works this way: one person speaks while the other listens, and then they switch. Therefore, option B is correct.
qs.rel: Half-duplex = both directions, one at a time: walkie-talkie, CB radio, hub-based Ethernet (CSMA/CD), Wi-Fi. Full-duplex examples: telephone, switched Ethernet. Simplex: TV, radio, keyboard, monitor. Only three standard modes exist.

qs.stem: _____ mode allows transmission in both directions simultaneously.
qs.sol: Mode that allows transmission in both directions simultaneously is:  Duplex (Full Duplex)
qs.rel: Duplex = full-duplex: simultaneous two-way, e.g. telephone and switched Ethernet (separate wire pairs). Capacity effectively doubles (100 Mbps each way). 'Half simplex' is not a mode. Full duplex needs no CSMA/CD.

qs.stem: _____ mode allows transmission in either direction but not simultaneously.
qs.sol:
Answer: Half Duplex allows transmission in either direction but not simultaneously.

Simplex — one-way only; example: TV broadcast or a keyboard sending data to a computer.

Half duplex — two-way but not at the same time; devices take turns transmitting; example: walkie‑talkies or a shared Ethernet hub.

Full duplex (Duplex) — two-way simultaneously; example: telephone calls or modern switched Ethernet links.

Note: The term "Half-Simplex" is not standard; use "Half Duplex" to describe two-way non-simultaneous transmission.
qs.rel: Half-duplex: transmit or receive but not both at once; needs turn-taking (collision handling). Examples: walkie-talkie, hub Ethernet, old CB radio. Simplex is one-way only; duplex both at once.

qs.stem: A connection that allows traffic either way, but only one way at a time is known as ______.
qs.sol:
Half duplex systems:

Devices can send and receive, but not at the same time

One device must wait while the other transmits
qs.rel: Half-duplex defined as 'either way, one at a time'. Remember ordering: simplex (1 direction) < half-duplex (2 directions alternately) < full-duplex (2 simultaneous). Shared medium LANs with hubs run half duplex.

qs.stem: Which data transmission technique in a computer network requires a dedicated communication channel?
qs.sol: Circuit switching reserves an end-to-end path for the duration of a connection. Packet and message switching share links as data units are forwarded. Hence the technique requiring a dedicated communication channel is circuit switching.
qs.rel: Circuit switching: setup, transfer, teardown phases with a dedicated path/reserved resources (PSTN telephone). Packet switching shares links by statistical multiplexing. Circuit gives constant delay, no per-message header, but wastes idle capacity.

qs.stem: Which of the following switching technique was used in ARPANET?
qs.sol: ARPANET utilized packet switching technology, which divides data into blocks for efficient network transmission. This approach distinguished it from earlier circuit and message switching methods.
qs.rel: ARPANET used packet switching (store-and-forward IMPs), the basis of the Internet. Packet switching: datagram (IP) vs virtual circuit (X.25, Frame Relay, ATM). Circuit switching dominated telephony, message switching telegraph/email relay.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are true regarding switching techniques in Data communication?
 Statements:
 I. In circuit switching a dedicated path is identified between the sender and the receiver.
 II. In packet switching each information to be transmitted between sender and receiver is broken down into smaller packets.
qs.sol:
Answer: Both statements are true.

Statement I: In circuit switching, a dedicated communication path is established between the sender and the receiver for the duration of the session. Resources along that path may be reserved, ensuring a constant connection (example: traditional circuit-switched telephone networks).

Statement II: In packet switching, the information to be transmitted is divided into smaller packets. Each packet carries header information (such as source and destination addresses) and packets can be routed independently through the network (example: Internet). Packet switching uses statistical multiplexing and does not require a dedicated path. …
qs.rel: Circuit switching: dedicated path; packet switching: message broken into packets with headers, each routed independently (datagram) or along a virtual circuit. Packets may arrive out of order and need reassembly. Message switching stores whole message at each node.

qs.stem: Communication of CPU with keyboard and monitor is an example of which of the following modes of communication?
qs.sol: Simplex communication is one-way communication. A keyboard sends input to the CPU, and a monitor receives output from the CPU; each direction is one-way. Hence the communication mode illustrated is simplex. Therefore, option A is correct.
qs.rel: Simplex = unidirectional: keyboard to CPU, CPU to monitor, radio/TV broadcast. Half-duplex needs reversing direction; full-duplex is simultaneous. Printer and sensors are also simplex examples.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are true regarding Data Communication?
Statements:
I. Half duplex communication is multidirectional communication.
II. Full duplex communication is bidirectional communication.
qs.sol:
Concept: Data-communication modes are classified along two independent axes: how many directions data can flow over a link, and whether both directions can be active at the same time. A two-endpoint link has exactly two possible flow directions (end A to end B, and end B to end A) — so the accepted direction-count terms in this classification are only “unidirectional” (one-way) and “bidirectional” (two-way). There is no separate “multidirectional” category in this taxonomy, because a single channel between two ends cannot carry more than two directions in the first place.

Simplex: one direction only (unidirectional) — e.g., keyboard to computer. …
qs.rel: Half-duplex is bidirectional but alternating (not 'multidirectional'); full-duplex is bidirectional simultaneously. A two-endpoint link has only two directions. Capacity of full duplex = 2 x half duplex link rate in aggregate.

qs.stem:
Which of the following is a type of transmission mode?

I. Simplex mode

II. Half simplex mode

III. Duplex mode
qs.sol:
Concept: Data communications defines exactly three transmission modes based on the direction and simultaneity of data flow between two devices — Simplex (data flows in one direction only), Half-duplex (data flows in both directions, but only one direction is active at a time), and Full-duplex (data flows in both directions simultaneously, often shortened to "Duplex"). No other named mode exists in this standard classification.

Application: Checking each Roman-numeral statement against this classification:

I. Simplex mode — matches the standard one-direction-only mode.

II. …
qs.rel: Valid modes: simplex, half-duplex, full-duplex (duplex). 'Half simplex' is a distractor. Link types by sharing: point-to-point vs multipoint. Wi-Fi radios are half-duplex; modern wired switched Ethernet is full-duplex.

qs.stem:
Which statement is correct regarding a point-to-point connection in data communication?

I. It provides a dedicated link between two devices.

II. It is a time-shared connection.
qs.sol:
Concept

A point-to-point configuration connects exactly two endpoints through a dedicated physical or logical link.

Time-sharing allocates a common communication resource among multiple users or devices at different times; it describes shared use rather than an exclusive endpoint-to-endpoint link.

For example, a direct link between two routers remains point-to-point even when packets are sent at different moments: the deciding issue is that the link capacity belongs to those two endpoints, not whether transmission is continuous.

Application

Statement I identifies a dedicated link between two devices, which matches the definition of a point-to-point connection. …
qs.rel: Point-to-point = dedicated link between exactly two devices, whole capacity reserved for them (e.g., leased line, PPP, serial link). Contrast multipoint/multidrop (bus) where capacity is shared. Mesh and star links are point-to-point.

qs.stem: Which of the following modes of communication is supported by Wi-Fi technology?
qs.sol:
Wi-Fi stations share a radio channel and ordinarily transmit or receive at a given instant.

This is half-duplex operation.
qs.rel: Wi-Fi (802.11) uses a shared radio channel with CSMA/CA, so it is half-duplex at the radio level. Full duplex over radio needs separate frequencies (FDD) as in cellular. Bluetooth uses TDD.

qs.stem: Which of the following is FALSE with respect to circuit-switched networks?

opts.A: A circuit-switched network is made of a set of switches connected by physical links
opts.B: Each of the physical links in the circuit-switched network within switched network is divided into n channels
opts.C: In a circuit-switched network, the resources need not be reserved during the setup phase
opts.D: In a circuit-switched network, the resources remain dedicated for the entire duration of data transfer

qs.sol:
Concept: Circuit switching provides a connection by allocating an end-to-end sequence of channels before data transfer. The allocated capacity is held for that connection until release, rather than being allocated independently for each packet.

A physical link can support multiple circuits using frequency bands or recurring time slots; a circuit uses one channel on each link of its route.

Consider a call from endpoint X through two switches to endpoint Y. During setup, the switches select a route and check for an available channel on every link.

If every required link has capacity, setup reserves the channels and connects them through the switches. …
qs.rel: Circuit-switched: each link divided into channels (FDM/TDM) and resources reserved for the call until teardown; not allocated on demand. Contrast packet switching. Setup delay exists, then no congestion for that call.

qs.stem: A walkie-talkie allows two people to communicate, but only one person can speak at a time while the other listens. This mode of data transmission is known as:
qs.sol: A walkie-talkie operates in Half-Duplex mode, allowing two-way communication where only one person speaks at a time. Simplex transmission is one-way only, while Full-Duplex permits simultaneous two-way communication. Multiplexing involves combining signals rather than defining transmission directionality.

qs.stem: A walkie-talkie allows two people to communicate, but only one person can speak at a time while the other listens. This mode of data transmission is known as:
qs.sol: A PAN is the smallest type of network and commonly uses Bluetooth or infrared for short-range communication.

qs.stem: Communication between a computer and a keyboard involves ____ transmission.

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Concept

Data-communication links are classified by the direction data can flow between two devices:

Simplex: data flows in exactly one direction only — one device always sends, the other always receives.

Half-duplex: data can flow in both directions, but only one direction at a time.

Full-duplex: data can flow in both directions at the same time.

Application

In the standard exam/textbook model of keyboard-computer communication, the keyboard is treated purely as an input device on this link: every keystroke travels from the keyboard to the computer, with no return data path used on that same channel for the computer to send instructions or data back to the keyboard. …

qs.stem: On what type of switching does Internet work?
qs.sol: The Internet is based on packet switching, where data is broken into packets and routed independently to the destination.

qs.stem: On what type of switching does Internet work?
qs.sol:
Answer: Gbps (gigabits per second).

Why this is correct: Internet connection speed measures how much data can be transferred per second, and is expressed in bits per second.

Common units: kilobits per second (kbps), megabits per second (Mbps), gigabits per second (Gbps).

Example: 100 Mbps means 100 megabits transferred each second; 1 Gbps means 1 gigabit per second.

Why the other choices are incorrect:

GHz (gigahertz) measures frequency (cycles per second), not data transfer rate.

DPI (dots per inch) measures image or print resolution and does not describe network speed.

PPM (pages per minute) refers to printing speed, not digital data transfer.

Communication between a computer and a keyboard is classified as simplex transmission. This is because data flows in only one direction, from the keyboard to the computer, without simultaneous return transmission.

qs.stem: What type of transmission is involved in communication between a computer and a keyboard?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
A keyboard sends keystrokes to the computer in the one-way communication model used by this classification.

That direction is simplex.

Correct answer: Packet switching

The modern Internet is designed around packet switching at the IP/data-communication level. Data is divided into packets; each packet can be routed independently and then reassembled at the destination.

Why not circuit switching? Circuit switching reserves a dedicated path for the whole session and is associated with traditional telephone networks. Some legacy access systems may use circuit-like mechanisms underneath, but the Internet’s core data communication is packet-switched. …

qs.stem: Which of the following switching techniques requires a dedicated communication path to be established between the sender and the receiver before any data transmission can take place?
qs.sol: Circuit switching requires the establishment of a dedicated communication path between the sender and receiver before any data transmission can occur. This ensures a constant connection for the duration of the communication session, unlike packet or message switching which do not require such a dedicated path.

qs.stem: Which switching technique establishes a dedicated physical path between source and destination nodes through intermediate nodes of communication network?
qs.sol:
Correct Answer: Circuit Switching

The question asks for a switching technique that establishes a dedicated physical path between the source and destination nodes. This is the defining characteristic of Circuit Switching.

Analysis of Options

Packet Switching: Data is divided into small packets that travel independently. No dedicated path is reserved; packets may take different routes.

Message Switching: Entire messages are stored at each node before being forwarded. It does not establish a continuous dedicated path.

Physical Switching: This is not a standard term used in data communication for switching techniques. …

qs.stem: Datagram networks are also referred to as ______ networks.
qs.sol:
Only Connectionless describes how datagram networks operate

Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are technologies, not network types

Connection-oriented is the opposite concept

qs.stem: Data transmission using multiple pathways simultaneously is known as:
qs.sol: Parallel transmission sends multiple bits over separate channels at the same time. Serial transmission sends bits successively over a channel; duplex describes transmission direction instead.

qs.stem: Which one of the following statements correctly describes Wavelength-Division Multiplexing (WDM)?

opts.A: WDM is used only with metallic transmission media.
opts.B: WDM combines multiple optical signals of different wavelengths onto a single optical fiber.
opts.C: WDM combines multiple digital signals using different time slots.
opts.D:
WDM combines multiple signals using different code sequences.

E

Question not attempted

qs.sol: Wavelength-division multiplexing carries several optical channels at different wavelengths through one optical fiber. A multiplexer combines them and a demultiplexer separates them at the far end.

qs.stem: Upward multiplexing involves:

opts.A: Combining multiple data streams into one
opts.B: Distributing data to different physical channels

qs.sol:
Multiplexing lets several data streams share one communication channel. In layered network models, upward multiplexing specifically means that several higher-layer (upper-layer) connections or data streams are combined and carried together over a single lower-layer connection, used when one lower-layer connection is shared by multiple upper-layer streams.

Applying this here: among the listed operations, only combining multiple data streams into one matches merging several upper-layer streams onto a single lower-layer channel. This is exactly what upward multiplexing means. …

qs.stem: In TDM, slots are further divided into

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
BPSC’s final answer key (08.12.2023 examination, Series A) gives "Frames". In TDM a frame is made of time slots and each slot carries bits, so a slot is not divided into frames; the answer shown is "Bits".

Concept

Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) organizes a shared channel's transmission time into a strict containment hierarchy: a TDM frame is divided into a fixed number of time slots (one slot per multiplexed input line), and under the standard synchronous-TDM convention, each individual slot carries a fixed-size unit of the sender's raw digital data — one or more bits. …

qs.stem: PSTN is an example of _________ network.
qs.sol: The public switched telephone network establishes a dedicated circuit for a call before data flows.

qs.stem: Find the transmission rate of circuit of the TDM where a link transmits 4000 frames per second and each slot has 8 bits respectively. TDM is
qs.sol:
Given:
Frames per second = 4000
Bits per slot = 8

Transmission rate = Frames/sec × Bits per frame
= 4000 × 8 = 32000 bps = 32 kbps

qs.stem: The number of crosspoints needed for 10 lines in a crosspoint switch, which is full duplex in nature and there is no self-connection, is
qs.sol:
Concept:

A crosspoint switch (a crossbar) lays its lines out as the rows and the columns of a matrix. At every row-column intersection sits one switching element, called a crosspoint, and closing that element joins the line on that row to the line on that column. The number of crosspoints is therefore simply the number of intersections the design actually has to build.

A crosspoint switch that serves a set of lines uses that same set as both its rows and its columns, so its matrix is symmetric about the diagonal; such a layout is called a triangular or two-way matrix. …

qs.stem: The number of crosspoints needed for 10 lines in a full-duplex directional crossbar switch, with separate switching elements for opposite directions and no self-connections, is —
qs.sol:
Modified from the original question: the architecture was unspecified; this stem explicitly requires separate directional switching elements, so the count is unique.

Each line can connect to nine other lines, giving ten ordered source–destination choices per set of nine.

The total is 10 × 9 = 90 crosspoints; a shared bidirectional element per unordered pair describes a different folded architecture.

qs.stem:
Consider a source computer(S) transmitting a file of size 106 bits to a destination computer(D) over a network of two routers (R1 and R2) and three links (L1, L2 and L3). L1 connects S to R1; L2 connects R1 to R2; and L3 connects R2 to D. Let each link be of length 100 km. Assume signals travel over each link at a speed of 108 meters per second. Assume that the link bandwidth on each link is 1 Mbps.

Let the file be broken down into 1000 packets each of size 1000 bits. Find the total sum of transmission and propagation delays in transmitting the file from S to D.

topics.deep:
- **Simplex:** one-way only, receiver cannot reply. Examples: **keyboard -> CPU, CPU -> monitor, TV/radio broadcast, printer**. **Half-duplex:** both directions but **one at a time** (shared channel): **walkie-talkie, CB radio, old Ethernet hub/CSMA-CD, Wi-Fi (802.11 radios transmit or receive at one time)**. **Full-duplex (duplex):** both directions **simultaneously**: telephone, modern switched Ethernet, mobile phone. 'Half simplex' and 'Multi-directional' are not standard modes; only **three** modes exist.
- **Link capacity:** full duplex doubles capacity (e.g., 100 Mbps in each direction). Uses two channels or two frequency/wire pairs.
- **Point-to-point:** dedicated link between exactly two devices; entire capacity reserved for them. Multipoint: shared among many.
- **Switching** = how data moves from source to destination through intermediate nodes. Classification: **Circuit switching**, **Message switching (store and forward)**, **Packet switching** (datagram and virtual-circuit approaches). Frame switching is not a standard class (frame relay is a packet technology).
- **Circuit switching:** three phases (**setup, data transfer, teardown**); **dedicated path** and resources reserved for the whole call; no header per message, in-order delivery, constant delay, no congestion once set up, but wasteful if idle, setup delay, a link failure drops the call. Example: PSTN telephone. Resources divided by **FDM or TDM**. Each physical link is divided into channels (so a link can carry many circuits). Resources are *not* released until teardown.
- **Message switching:** whole message stored at each node then forwarded; no setup; high delay; needs big buffers; used in telegram/email (store-forward).
- **Packet switching:** message broken into **packets**; each carries header (source, destination, sequence); statistical multiplexing; efficient utilisation; variable delay/jitter; packets may be lost or arrive out of order. **Datagram** = connectionless, each packet routed independently (IP). **Virtual circuit** = connection set up first, fixed path, packets carry VC id (X.25, Frame Relay, ATM, MPLS). **ARPANET** and the Internet use packet switching.
- **Delay in circuit switching:** setup + propagation + transmission. In packet switching with n hops, message L bits, packet p bits: total ≈ (n−1)·(p/R) + L/R (store-and-forward pipelining). Example: 1 packet of 1000 bits at 1 Mbps over 3 hops = 3 ms transmission.
- **Comparison table:**
| Feature | Circuit | Packet (datagram) | Message |
|---|---|---|---|
| Path | dedicated | per-packet | per-message |
| Setup | yes | no | no |
| Delay | constant | variable | high |
| Efficiency | low | high | medium |
| Typical | telephone | Internet | telegram/email |
- **Wireless modes:** Wi-Fi is half-duplex per radio; cellular uses FDD/TDD to simulate full duplex; Bluetooth uses TDD.
- **Common traps:** 'Half duplex is multidirectional' is false (it is bidirectional, one at a time); only full duplex is simultaneous bidirectional. 'Duplex' alone = full-duplex. Circuit switching does NOT mean a physical wire per call; shared links hold many circuits, while the circuit's share is reserved. In circuit switching, resources are NOT allocated on demand.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) mode for TV broadcast, telephone, chat room, Ethernet hub; (2) 3 phases of circuit switching; (3) which uses store-and-forward; (4) datagram vs virtual circuit; (5) X.25/Frame relay/ATM classification; (6) delay calculation for a packet-switched path; (7) why packet switching gives better utilisation; (8) which switching needs header on every unit; (9) bandwidth of full duplex vs half duplex link; (10) which switching suffers congestion/packet loss.

topics.title: 3. Signals, Bandwidth, Impairments & Modulation
topics.theory:
- **Digital signal = analog (continuous) data represented in discrete form**; analog signal is continuous.
- **Bandwidth (Hz)** = range of frequencies a channel/composite signal covers. **Bandwidth (bps)** = max data rate/capacity of a link ("capacity of link = bandwidth"). Delay terms (latency, transit time) are different.
- **Baud rate (signal rate)** = signal elements/second; **bit rate** = bits/second; bit rate = baud × bits per signal element.
- **Sine wave parameters:** peak amplitude, frequency, phase. **Wavelength is derived:** λ = propagation speed × period = speed / frequency.
- **Impairments:** *Attenuation* = loss of energy/strength with distance (cured by amplifiers/repeaters) · *Distortion* = change of signal shape · *Noise* = unwanted extra energy. Wireless: **path loss** = power falls with distance.
- **Bits in the link (delay × bandwidth product)** = Bandwidth × propagation delay, where delay = length / speed. e.g. 100 km, 2×10⁸ m/s, 1.536 Mbps → 0.5 ms × 1.536 Mbps = **768 bits**.
- Formulas to memorise: Nyquist (noiseless) C = 2B·log₂L · Shannon (noisy) C = B·log₂(1+S/N).
- **Modulation (digital→analog):** ASK (amplitude; On-Off Keying), FSK (frequency), PSK (phase), QAM/QPSK. Identify by *which feature of the carrier changes*.
- **Line coding:** Manchester has a transition in the **middle of every bit** (self-synchronising); pulse width is **half** of straight binary; needs twice the bandwidth; used in classic Ethernet.
- **Multiplexing:** many-to-one combines low-speed lines into one high-speed line (MUX); **demultiplexing is one-to-many**. Types FDM, TDM, **WDM (wavelength, fibre)**, CDMA (code). WDMA = Wavelength Division Multiple Access.
- MPEG standard is a **bitstream** specification (syntax of compressed stream + decoder).

qs.stem: The capacity of the link is known as __________ of the link.
qs.sol:
Concept

In data communication, the bandwidth of a link is the maximum rate at which data can be carried across that link. "Capacity" and "bandwidth" describe the same property of the channel: the upper limit on how much data the link can transfer per unit time. So the capacity of a link is simply its bandwidth.

Applying it here

The blank asks for the term that names a link's data-carrying capacity. That term is bandwidth, because bandwidth is defined precisely as the maximum amount of data a link can transmit in a given time. A higher-bandwidth link can move more bits per second, i.e. it has a larger capacity.

Capacity vs. …
qs.rel: Bandwidth (bps) = capacity of link; throughput = achieved rate. Bandwidth-delay product = bandwidth x propagation delay = bits in transit (1 Mbps x 20 ms = 20,000 bits). Bandwidth in Hz is the frequency span of a channel.

qs.stem: The loss of energy as a signal propagates outward is known as ______.
qs.sol:
Concept. A transmission medium is never perfect, so every signal that crosses it is degraded on the way. The classical transmission impairments are separated by what they change about the signal: its power (how strong it is), its shape (how its frequency components line up in time), or its content (what extra energy has been mixed into it).

Application. The stem describes energy being lost while the signal travels outward, so the property that changes is the signal's power. The impairment defined as a fall in signal power over distance is Attenuation: as the wave propagates, the resistance of the medium converts part of its energy into heat, so less power arrives than was launched. …
qs.rel: Attenuation = loss of signal strength with distance, fixed by amplifiers/repeaters, measured in dB. Distortion = shape change from unequal frequency delays; noise = added unwanted signal (thermal, crosstalk, impulse). Wireless equivalent: path loss.

qs.stem: The MPEG standard is primarily a _____ specification?
qs.sol:
Concept: MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group) standards do not standardize how a video or audio encoder is built. The committee's actual deliverable is the syntax and semantics of the compressed data stream and the matching decoding process — in other words, the format of the bitstream — so that any compliant decoder can correctly interpret data produced by any compliant encoder.

Application: Applying this to the given item: the MPEG standard defines exactly how compressed audio/video data is organised into a stream of bits (frame headers, motion vectors, quantised coefficients, and so on) and how a decoder must interpret that stream. …
qs.rel: MPEG (Moving Picture Experts Group) defines compressed audio/video as a bitstream specification; MP3 = MPEG-1 Layer III; JPEG is for still images. Related: lossy vs lossless compression, codecs.

qs.stem: When a signal travels through a media, loss in its energy is called:
qs.sol: Attenuation refers to the reduction in signal strength or energy as it propagates through a transmission medium. This phenomenon occurs due to absorption, scattering, or dispersion within the material.
qs.rel: Attenuation: energy loss in medium; repeaters regenerate digital signals, amplifiers boost analog (and noise). Shielded cables still attenuate; shielding only reduces EMI. Latency is a delay measure, not energy loss.

qs.stem: Number of signal elements transmitted per second is called ____.
qs.sol:
Concept: In data communication, the signal rate (baud rate) is the number of signal elements (symbols) sent per second, measured in baud. A signal element is the smallest unit of a transmitted signal — one constant level of voltage, phase, or frequency. This is separate from the data rate (bit rate), which counts bits per second.

Application: The phrase “number of signal elements transmitted per second” is the exact textbook definition of the baud rate, so the term being defined here is the baud rate.

Contrast with the other terms:

Bit rate — bits per second, i.e. data volume, not symbols. If each symbol carries n bits, bit rate = baud rate × n. …
qs.rel: Baud = signal elements/s; bit rate = baud x bits per element (1000 baud at 4 bits/element = 4000 bps). QAM/QPSK carry multiple bits per baud. Nyquist: C = 2B log2 L; Shannon: C = B log2(1 + S/N).

qs.stem: _________ is a device that combines a large number of low speed transmission lines into a high speed line.
qs.sol: A multiplexer (MUX) is a device that combines multiple low-speed transmission lines into a single high-speed line. This process allows for efficient data transmission by aggregating signals.
qs.rel: Multiplexer combines many low-speed inputs onto one high-speed link (many-to-one); demultiplexer reverses. Kinds: FDM, TDM (synchronous/statistical), WDM, CDM. Switches/repeaters are different jobs.

qs.stem: What is the full form of WDMA protocol?
qs.sol:
WDMA = Wavelength Division Multiple Access

Allows multiple users to transmit data simultaneously using different light wavelengths

Each wavelength acts like a separate channel
qs.rel: WDMA = Wavelength Division Multiple Access; WDM sends different wavelengths (colours) over one fibre, DWDM is dense. FDM is the analog-frequency equivalent. Compare FDMA, TDMA, CDMA multiple-access schemes.

qs.stem: Multiplexing follows __________ approach, whereas demultiplexing follows __________ approach.
qs.sol: Multiplexing is a many-to-one technique because several signals or data streams are combined and sent over a single communication channel. Demultiplexing performs the reverse operation, separating one combined stream into multiple output streams. Therefore, the correct pair is many-to-one; one-to-many, so option D is correct.
qs.rel: Multiplexing is many-to-one at the sender; demultiplexing is one-to-many at the receiver. The same terms apply at the transport layer (ports demultiplex segments to processes). Sharing of one link, not duplication of signals.

qs.stem: In Ethernet, when Manchester encoding is used, then the pulse width are ____ of the straight binary encoding.
qs.sol: In Manchester encoding, each bit period is divided into two halves to ensure synchronization. A transition occurs in the middle of every bit, meaning the duration of a single signal level (pulse width) is half the bit period. In contrast, straight binary encoding maintains a constant level for the entire bit period. Therefore, the pulse width in Manchester encoding is half that of straight binary encoding.
qs.rel: Manchester: transition in the middle of every bit (low-to-high = 1 in IEEE 802.3), self-clocking, but needs twice the bandwidth because pulses are half-width. Used in 10 Mbps Ethernet; Differential Manchester in Token Ring; Fast Ethernet uses 4B/5B.

qs.stem: In networking, the bandwidth in hertz refers to:

opts.A: The range of frequencies in a composite signal or the range of frequencies that a channel can pass
opts.B: The speed of bit transmission in a channel or link
opts.C: The time required for a bit to travel from the source to the destination
opts.D: The time it takes for an entire message to completely arrive at the destination

qs.sol:
Bandwidth measured in hertz is the width of a frequency range. Bit rate is measured in bits per second, while the other descriptions are delays.

A frequency range is measured in hertz.
qs.rel: Bandwidth in Hz = range of frequencies (fmax - fmin). Example: telephone voice 300-3400 Hz = 3100 Hz usable, nominal 4 kHz. In bps it means capacity. Don't confuse with latency (time) or throughput.

qs.stem: To obtain figure (b) from figure (a) in a binary system, which modulation technique is applied?
qs.sol:
Concept. A carrier wave has three features: height (amplitude), spacing between cycles (frequency), and where a cycle begins (phase).

Modulation changes a feature to carry information. To name the technique, find which feature changes; you do not need to count every wave.

Apply this to the two drawings. The upper drawing (a) is the bit signal. The lower drawing (b) is the wave carrying it.

Look at the height of wave (b): its peaks and troughs stay about the same height, so height is not the changing feature.

Look at the spacing: some cycles are close together and others are farther apart. Closer cycles mean higher frequency; wider spacing means lower frequency. …
qs.rel: Figure-based: frequency of the carrier changes with the data bit = FSK. ASK changes amplitude, PSK phase, QAM both amplitude and phase. ASK is most noise-sensitive. QPSK sends 2 bits per symbol.

qs.stem: Which modulation technique is applied to a binary signal in figure (a) to achieve figure (b)?
qs.sol:
In figure (b), we can see that the carrier wave changes its amplitude (its height/strength) based on the binary input from figure (a):

Binary '1': A carrier sine wave is present at a specific amplitude.

Binary '0': The carrier wave is absent (the amplitude is zero).

This specific type of AM, where the carrier is switched completely "on" or "off," is often called On-Off Keying (OOK).
qs.rel: Figure-based: amplitude of carrier changes with bits = ASK (on/off keying is the simplest case). Compare FSK (frequency), PSK (phase). Digital-to-analog conversion uses these; analog-to-digital uses PCM (sampling >= 2 fmax).

qs.stem: A digital signal is a representation of _______ data in _________ form.
qs.sol:
A digital signal represents analog data in discrete form.

Analog data: continuous data that can vary smoothly over time.

Discrete form: separate levels or values used in digital representation.

Therefore, the correct pair is analog, discrete.
qs.rel: Digital signal = discrete representation of analog data (sampling and quantisation in PCM). 8 kHz sampling x 8 bits = 64 kbps for voice. Analog signal is continuous; data can be either, signals either.

qs.stem: Which of the following is correct formula for calculating wavelength (λ) of a signal in the data communication?
qs.sol: Wavelength equals propagation speed divided by frequency. Since period is the reciprocal of frequency, wavelength also equals propagation speed multiplied by period.
qs.rel: Wavelength = propagation speed x period (= speed/frequency). Period T = 1/f. Light in vacuum 3x10^8 m/s; in cable about 2/3 of that. Example: f = 1 MHz in cable at 2x10^8 m/s gives 200 m.

qs.stem: In periodic analog signals, which of the following is NOT a parameter to describe a sine wave in data communication?
qs.sol:
Concept

A periodic analog signal is built from sine waves, and a single sine wave is completely described by exactly three independent parameters: peak amplitude (its maximum value, i.e. the strength of the signal), frequency (the number of cycles it completes per second, in hertz), and phase (its position in the cycle at time zero, measured in degrees or radians).

Wavelength is a derived, spatial quantity: it is the distance a single cycle occupies as the wave travels through a medium, and it equals propagation speed divided by frequency. …
qs.rel: Sine wave parameters: peak amplitude, frequency (period) and phase. Wavelength is derived from speed and period. Phase is measured in degrees/radians; frequency in Hz; amplitude in volts.

qs.stem: In wireless communication, radio waves at low frequencies pass through obstacles well, but the power falls off sharply with distance from the source. This attenuation is called ______.
qs.sol:
Path loss is the attenuation of radio-wave power as propagation distance increases.

It arises from spreading and environmental effects along the propagation path.
qs.rel: Path loss = power falloff with distance in wireless; low-frequency radio penetrates obstacles but is omnidirectional with heavy path loss; microwaves are line-of-sight and high-frequency waves are absorbed. Free-space loss grows with distance squared and frequency.

qs.stem: Suppose a 100 km long cable has a speed of 1.536 Mbps. The signal speed in cable is 2/3 speed of the light. What will be the number of bits in the cable?
qs.sol: Calculate signal speed as two-thirds of light speed, yielding 200 million meters per second. Determine propagation delay by dividing the 100-kilometer cable length by this speed, resulting in half a millisecond. Multiply the 1.536 Mbps bandwidth by this delay to find exactly 768 bits in the cable.
qs.rel: Bandwidth-delay product: delay = 100 km / 2x10^8 = 0.5 ms; bits = 1.536 Mbps x 0.5 ms = 768. Change distance or speed ratio and the answer scales linearly; this is the 'pipe capacity' for window sizing.

qs.stem: The default baud rate of Modbus RTU is?
qs.sol:
Modified from the official paper: the stem now specifies a regular-class device with the recommended rate implemented, because Modbus RTU has no universal device-independent default.

The implementation guide recommends 19200 bit/s for a regular-class device when that rate is implemented; 9600 bit/s is the fallback when it is not. Under the stated condition, the recommended rate is 19200 bit/s.

qs.stem: The default baud rate of Modbus RTU is?
qs.sol: Bluetooth links devices over a short personal range around one user. A network at that scale is a personal area network, abbreviated PAN. It is smaller in scope than a local, metropolitan or wide area network.

Network bandwidth is a measurement indicating the maximum capacity of a wired or wireless communication link to transmit data over a network connection in a given amount of time. Bandwidth is represented in the number of bits, kilobits, megabits, or gigabits that can be transmitted in one second.

qs.stem: The term used to describe the maximum amount of data that can be transmitted over a communication channel in a given time period is:
qs.sol: Bandwidth represents the maximum capacity of a communication channel—how much data can be transmitted per unit time under ideal conditions.

qs.stem: The delay that occur during the playback of a stream is called ___________
qs.sol: In streaming, jitter is the variation in packet delivery delay. When packets arrive at uneven intervals, the player can experience irregular timing or pauses; a playback buffer absorbs some of that variation.

qs.stem: एक मोडबस टीसीपी पैके ट में लेनदेन पहचानकर्ता का डिफ़ॉल्ट मान है?
qs.sol:
आधिकारिक उत्तर-कुंजी पर टिप्पणी: बोर्ड की आधिकारिक उत्तर-कुंजी विकल्प “1” को सही मानती है। कोई भी छपा विकल्प पूरी तरह तर्कसंगत नहीं है, क्योंकि Modbus TCP का transaction identifier क्लाइंट तय करता है; प्रोटोकॉल कोई सार्वभौमिक डिफ़ॉल्ट नहीं देता। इस प्रश्न का मूल्यांकन आधिकारिक कुंजी के अनुसार किया गया है, जैसा वास्तविक परीक्षा में हुआ।

क्लाइंट अनुरोध और उत्तर मिलाने के लिए पहचानकर्ता रखता है; सर्वर वही लौटाता है। कोई निश्चित संख्या डिफ़ॉल्ट नहीं है।

qs.stem: In Real Time Interactive Audio Video, Jitter is introduced in real-time data by delay between____
qs.sol: Jitter is variation in the time interval between arrival of successive network packets. Uneven packet delay makes real-time audio or video play irregularly unless a jitter buffer smooths it.

qs.stem: Under the Modbus over Serial Line specification, what default baud rate is recommended for a Regular-class implementation?
qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: Modbus RTU devices can be configured at several rates, so the stem now names the specification’s Regular-class recommendation. The Modbus serial-line guide specifies a default of 19200 baud for that class; other supported rates do not change the stated default.

The transaction identifier in a Modbus TCP packet is a 16-bit field used to match requests and responses. According to the Modbus TCP specification, the default value for this field is 1. This value is used when a new transaction starts to ensure that the request and response can be correctly matched during communication.

हिन्दी उत्तर: Modbus TCP पैकेट में ट्रांजैक्शन आइडेंटिफायर एक 16-बिट फील्ड होता है जो अनुरोध और प्रतिक्रिया को मैच करने के लिए उपयोग किया जाता है। Modbus TCP निर्देशावली के अनुसार, इस फील्ड का डिफ़ॉल्ट मान 1 होता है। यह मान तब उपयोग किया जाता है जब एक नया लेनदेन शुरू होता है ताकि अनुरोध और प्रतिक्रिया को संचार के दौरान सही ढंग से मैच किया जा सके।

qs.stem: Determine the maximum length of the cable (in km) for transmitting data at a rate of 500 Mbps in an Ethernet LAN with frames of size 10000 bits. Assume the signal speed in the cable to be 200000 km/s.
qs.sol: For Ethernet CSMA/CD, transmission time must exceed twice the propagation delay. Using distance equals frame size times speed divided by two times bandwidth, we calculate 10000 bits times 200000 km/s divided by two times 500 Mbps. This results in a maximum cable length of exactly 2 kilometers.

qs.stem: What will be the path loss in dB for an open air site?
qs.sol:
In wireless communication, path loss refers to the reduction in signal strength as it travels through open air (free space). Using the Free-space Path Loss formula, path loss is expressed as a positive value in dB, because it indicates loss.

A value like 80.27 dB is realistic for open-air/mobile communication systems, while negative values are not used to represent path loss.

qs.stem: Which type of channel does not represent any correlation between input and output symbols?
qs.sol: A Useless Channel is a channel where the output symbols have no relation (no correlation) to the input symbols. This means the received output gives no information about what was sent.

qs.stem: Which type of channel does not represent any correlation between input and output symbols?
qs.sol: A distributed system consists of multiple computers that appear as a single coherent system to clients. This distinguishes it from standard networks where distribution is visible.

qs.stem: Nyquist theorem to calculate the data rate is:
qs.sol: The Nyquist theorem defines the maximum data rate for a noiseless channel as 2B log₂(V) bits per second, where B is the bandwidth in Hertz and V is the number of signal levels. Option 3 correctly represents this formula as '2 H log₂ V bits/sec', assuming H stands for bandwidth.

qs.stem: According to the Nyquist theorem, the sampling rate must be:
qs.sol:
Concept: A digital signature binds message content to a signer through a cryptographic digest and a signature made with the signer’s private key.

Integrity is checked by recomputing the digest from the received message and verifying the signature with the signer’s public key. If the message changes, its digest ordinarily changes.

The signer computes a hash of the original message, obtaining a digest tied to those message bytes.

The signer signs that digest with the signing private key. The recipient computes a fresh digest from the received message.

Verification compares the freshly computed digest with the digest authenticated by the signature. …

Answer:  Sampling
 Sampling is the process of taking measurements of the amplitude of a continuous waveform at regular time intervals. Each measured value (sample) can then be quantized to discrete levels and encoded as a binary number to produce a digital representation of the original signal.
 Sampling rate: determines how often snapshots are taken (higher rates capture more detail).

qs.stem: A communication channel has a bandwidth of 1 MHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of 127. The maximum achievable data rate of the channel is:
qs.sol: Shannon capacity is C = B log2(1 + S/N). With B = 1 MHz and S/N = 127, 1 + S/N = 128 = 2^7, hence C = 1,000,000 × 7 bits/s = 7 Mbps.

qs.stem: According to the Nyquist theorem, the sampling rate must be:

opts.A: Four times the bandwidth of the signal
opts.B: Equal to the highest frequency contained in the signal
opts.C: Half of the highest frequency contained in the signal
opts.D:
At least twice the highest frequency contained in the signal

E

Question not attempted

qs.sol: For a band-limited signal with highest frequency f_max, the Nyquist sampling condition is f_s ≥ 2f_max. Sampling slower allows spectral replicas to overlap and causes aliasing.

qs.stem: As per Nyquist theorem, to reproduce the original analog signal one necessary condition is that the sampling rate be at least ……… the highest frequency present in the original signal.
qs.sol:
If a continuous-time (analog) signal contains frequency components only up to a maximum frequency fₘₐₓ, then perfect reconstruction from samples requires:

fₛ ≥ 2fₘₐₓ

where fₛ is the sampling frequency.

If fₛ < 2fₘₐₓ, the replicated spectra overlap. This is aliasing, and the original signal cannot be uniquely recovered.

If fₛ ≥ 2fₘₐₓ, the spectra remain separate and an ideal low-pass filter can reconstruct the original signal.

qs.stem: A signal has a power of 100 W at Point 1 and 10 W at Point 2. What is the attenuation of the signal in decibels (dB)? (Choose the most appropriate option from below)
qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: the power falls tenfold, so the original choices contained no positive attenuation magnitude; the negative decibel change was replaced by the positive attenuation magnitude. Attenuation as a loss is 10 log10(P_in/P_out) = 10 log10(100/10) = 10 dB. The signed change in level would instead be −10 dB.

qs.stem: How many characters per second (7 bits + 1 parity) can be transmitted over a 2400 bps line if the transfer is asynchronous (1 start and 1 stop bit)?
qs.sol: Each asynchronous character occupies seven data bits, one parity bit, one start bit and one stop bit: ten bits. At 2400 bits per second, the character rate is 2400 ÷ 10 = 240 per second.

qs.stem: Quantizing noise occurs in –
qs.sol: Quantizing noise is an inherent error introduced when continuous analog signal amplitudes are mapped to discrete digital levels. This phenomenon is specific to Pulse Code Modulation (PCM) systems where analog-to-digital conversion occurs. Multiplexing techniques like TDM and FDM do not inherently cause quantization errors.

qs.stem: A signal of 5 kHz is used to modulate a carrier of frequency 1 MHz using amplitude modulation. The frequencies of side bands will be:
qs.sol:
Key point:  Step-index fibers have a uniform (constant) core refractive index from center to edge; graded-index fibers have a refractive index that decreases gradually from the center toward the edge.
 Multimode step-index fiber — Intended correct answer: The core refractive index is constant across the core, with an abrupt drop at the cladding. Light is guided by total internal reflection, and this profile is the classic example of a constant core density.

qs.stem: A signal of 5 kHz is used to modulate a carrier of frequency 1 MHz using amplitude modulation. The frequencies of side bands will be:
qs.sol: AM sidebands lie at carrier ± modulating frequency: 1 MHz ± 0.005 MHz gives 1.005 and 0.995 MHz.

qs.stem: The —— measures the number of lost or garbled messages as a fraction of the total sent in the sampling period.

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Concept

Network service-quality (QoS) parameters describe how reliably a connection delivers data. Among these, the residual error rate is defined as the fraction of messages that arrive lost or garbled out of the total messages sent, measured over a fixed sampling period. In short, it is an accuracy metric: residual error rate = (lost or garbled messages) / (total messages sent).

Applying it here

The stem describes a metric that counts lost or corrupted messages as a fraction of the total sent during a sampling window. That is precisely the definition of the residual error rate, so the blank is filled by "residual error rate". …

qs.stem: What is the maximum number of characters (7 bits + parity) that can be transmitted in a second on a 19.2 kbps line? This asynchronous transmission requires 1 start bit and 1 stop bit.
qs.sol:
Concept

In asynchronous character transmission, every character occupies a complete frame. The frame length is the sum of its data bits, parity bit, start bit, and stop bit.

The maximum character rate equals the line rate in bits per second divided by the number of transmitted bits in one character frame.

Application

The payload has 7 data bits and 1 parity bit, so the information portion uses 7 + 1 = 8 bits.

Adding 1 start bit and 1 stop bit gives a frame length of 8 + 1 + 1 = 10 bits per character.

The line rate is 19.2 kbps = 19,200 bits per second.

Maximum character rate = 19,200 ÷ 10 = 1,920 characters per second. …

qs.stem: An analog signal carries 4 bits in each signal unit. If 1000 signal units are sent per second, then baud rate and bit rate of the signal are ______ and ______.
qs.sol:
Concept: Baud rate counts transmitted signal units (symbols) per second. Bit rate counts transmitted bits per second.

For a fixed number of bits per signal unit, bit rate = symbol rate × bits per signal unit; these rates measure different quantities.

The given signal-unit rate is 1000 units per second, so the baud rate is 1000 baud. One baud already means one signal unit per second.

Each unit carries 4 bits. In one second, 1000 units carry 1000 × 4 = 4000 bits, so the bit rate is 4000 bps.

Cross-check: 4000 bits per second ÷ 1000 signal units per second = 4 bits per unit, reproducing the given payload. By contrast, counting bits as signal units would interchange the two measures. …

qs.stem: An analog signal carries 4 bits in each signal unit. If 1000 signal units are sent per second, then baud rate and bit rate of the signal are ______ and ______.
qs.sol: To determine the length of a UDP datagram, we start with the total length of the IP packet, which includes the IP header and the payload. The payload contains the UDP header and the UDP data. Therefore, the UDP length can be calculated by subtracting the IP header length from the total IP length. This gives the length of the UDP datagram, including the UDP header.

qs.stem: There are several common terminologies used for signal rate in the literature of computer networks. Which of the following is not a common terminology for signal rate?
qs.sol:
Period T=1000 ms=1 second

Frequency f=1/T

=1/1

= 1 Hz

Convert Hz to kHz:

1 Hz=10 -3

qs.stem: There are several common terminologies used for signal rate in the literature of computer networks. Which of the following is not a common terminology for signal rate?
qs.sol: Signal rate counts signal elements per second, whereas data rate counts bits per second. One signal element can encode more than one bit, making the two rates distinct.

qs.stem: In the __________ encoding scheme, each 24 bits become four 6-bit chunks, and eventually are sent as 32 bits.
qs.sol: Base64 converts 24-bit binary data into four 6-bit chunks, representing them as printable ASCII characters for safe data transmission.

qs.stem: Calculate the required bit rate of a channel if we need to download a text document at the rate of 100 pages per minute. Assume that a page has 24 lines with 80 characters in each line and one character is represented using 8 bits :
qs.sol: The official HTET 2022 final key (Set A) awarded marks to all candidates for this question, because none of the printed rates is the required one. Required rate: 24 lines × 80 characters × 8 bits = 15,360 bits per page. At 100 pages per minute that is 1,536,000 bits per minute, and dividing by 60 seconds gives 25,600 bits per second = 25.6 kbps. None of the four printed rates equals 25.6 kbps.

qs.stem: If the channel band is limited to 6 kHz and signal to noise ratio is 16, what would be the capacity of channel?
qs.sol: Shannon capacity is C = B log₂(1 + SNR). Substituting B = 6000 Hz and SNR = 16 gives C = 6000 log₂(17) ≈ 24.52 kbps. The printed value 24.74 kbps is the nearest listed approximation.

qs.stem: Which of the following techniques is used for transmitting digital signal?
qs.sol:
Answer: Amplitude Shift Keying (ASK)
 ASK is a digital modulation technique in which the amplitude of a carrier is switched between discrete levels to represent binary data (for example, one amplitude for binary '1' and another for binary '0'). Because ASK places digital symbols onto a carrier by changing amplitude levels, it is used to transmit digital signals over a channel.
 Why amplitude modulation (AM) is not correct: AM is an analog modulation technique that varies carrier amplitude continuously to convey analog information; it is not a digital modulation scheme.

qs.stem: What is Delta Modulation? (Choose the most appropriate option from below)

opts.A: An analog-to-digital conversion technique that encodes the difference between successive sample values.
opts.B: An analog-to-digital conversion technique in which each sample is encoded independently using multiple bits.
opts.C: A multiplexing technique that combines multiple analog signals into one channel.
opts.D:
A modulation technique that varies the frequency of a carrier signal.

E

Question not attempted

qs.sol: Delta modulation samples an analog signal and represents the direction of change relative to the preceding reconstructed sample with a one-bit step. It therefore encodes a difference rather than a full independent sample value.

topics.deep:
- **Analog** signal = continuous values (sine wave); **digital** = discrete levels (binary 0/1). Data may be analog/digital; signals likewise. **Periodic** signals repeat; non-periodic do not.
- **Sine wave parameters:** **peak amplitude**, **frequency f** (cycles/s, Hz), **phase**. **Period T = 1/f**. Wavelength is derived (λ = propagation speed × period = v/f), not a basic parameter. Light in vacuum 3×10^8 m/s. Phase measured in degrees/radians.
- **Bandwidth:** (a) in Hz = range of frequencies a channel/signal occupies (fmax − fmin); (b) in bps = link capacity/max data rate. 'Capacity of the link' = bandwidth. **Throughput** = actual rate achieved (<= bandwidth). **Latency** = propagation + transmission + queuing + processing. **Propagation delay** = distance/speed; **transmission delay** = L/R. **Bandwidth-delay product = bandwidth × propagation delay** = bits in flight 'in the pipe'. Worked example: 1 Mbps link, 20 ms one-way delay -> 20,000 bits.
- **Bit rate vs baud rate:** baud = signal elements/second; bit rate = baud × bits per element. 4 bits/element at 1000 baud = 4000 bps. (Baud rate <= bit rate.)
- **Capacity limits:** **Nyquist** (noiseless) C = 2B log2(L) bps; **Shannon** (noisy) C = B log2(1 + S/N). Example: B = 3 kHz, S/N = 1023 -> C = 3000 × 10 = 30 kbps. dB = 10 log10(S/N). Nyquist with 4 levels and 3 kHz: 2×3000×2 = 12 kbps.
- **Transmission impairments:** **Attenuation** (loss of energy with distance; fixed by amplifiers/repeaters; measured in dB), **Distortion** (signal shape change because different frequencies travel at different speeds), **Noise** (unwanted signal: thermal, induced, crosstalk, impulse). **Path loss** = power falloff with distance in wireless. SNR = signal power/noise power. Shielding reduces interference but **does not remove attenuation**.
- **Digital encoding (line coding):** NRZ-L, NRZ-I, RZ, **Manchester** (transition in middle of every bit; used in 10 Mbps Ethernet 802.3; clock embedded; **needs twice the bandwidth**, i.e., pulse width is half of straight binary), **Differential Manchester** (Token Ring 802.5), AMI, 4B/5B (Fast Ethernet), 8B/10B (Gigabit).
- **Modulation (digital data -> analog signal):** **ASK** (amplitude varies, most noise-prone), **FSK** (frequency varies), **PSK** (phase varies), **QPSK** (2 bits per symbol, 4 phases), **QAM** (amplitude + phase combined, used in modems/cable/Wi-Fi). **Analog modulation:** AM, FM, PM. **PCM** converts analog to digital: sampling (>= 2×fmax, Nyquist), quantization, encoding. Telephone voice 4 kHz -> 8000 samples/s × 8 bits = 64 kbps.
- **Multiplexing:** many-to-one at sender (**MUX** combines many low-speed lines into one high-speed link); **demultiplexing** is one-to-many at the receiver. Types: **FDM** (analog, frequency bands, guard bands), **TDM** (synchronous: fixed slots; statistical: slots on demand), **WDM** (optical, different wavelengths; **DWDM** dense), **CDM/CDMA** (codes). WDMA = Wavelength Division Multiple Access.
- **Comparison table:**
| Term | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Bandwidth (Hz) | frequency range | Hz |
| Bandwidth (digital) | max rate | bps |
| Throughput | actual rate | bps |
| Baud | symbols/s | baud |
| Latency | total delay | s |
- **Standards:** MPEG is a **bitstream** specification for compressed video/audio; JPEG images; MP3 = MPEG-1 Layer 3.
- **Common traps:** wavelength = speed × period (or speed/frequency), never sum; digital signal is a representation of analog data in discrete form; baud and bit rate differ unless 1 bit/symbol; amplitude not an 'impairment'.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) Shannon capacity calculation; (2) Nyquist rate for given bandwidth/levels; (3) bandwidth-delay product; (4) sampling rate for 5 kHz signal; (5) bit rate from baud and levels; (6) which encoding self-clocks; (7) FDM vs TDM vs WDM; (8) which modulation changes only phase; (9) SNR in dB conversion; (10) causes of noise types (crosstalk, thermal).

topics.title: 4. Transmission Media & Network Devices
topics.theory:
- **Guided (wired):** twisted pair (UTP/STP; **electrical current**; **RJ45**), coaxial (**RG** ratings e.g. RG-6/59; BNC), optical fibre (light). **Unguided (wireless):** radio, microwave, infrared, light, satellite. Propagation modes: ground, sky, line-of-sight.
- Shielded twisted pair **still suffers attenuation** (shield cuts interference, not attenuation). Fibre is faster/higher bandwidth than copper.
- **Optical fibre modes:** single-mode vs multimode (number of paths); step-index vs graded-index (refractive-index profile). "Ungraded index" is not a term.
- **Devices by OSI layer:** Repeater/Hub/Amplifier = **Layer 1 (Physical)** · Bridge/Switch = **Layer 2 (Data link)** · Router = **Layer 3 (Network)** · Gateway = Transport/Application (protocol conversion).
- A hub copies signal to all ports (one collision domain). Router connects *different networks* (not LAN segments — that is a bridge/switch), examines IP addresses, has filtering capability; router = *Internet layer* in TCP/IP.

qs.stem: Which of the following is not an example of Guided transmission media?
qs.sol:
Guided transmission media use physical pathways to transmit signals. Let's analyze each option:

A. Fiber optic: Uses light to transmit data through glass or plastic fibers. Signals are confined within the medium, making it a guided transmission medium.

B. Infrared wave: Transmits data through air using electromagnetic waves without a physical medium. This is an unguided transmission method.

C. Twisted pair: Uses copper wires twisted together to reduce interference. Signals travel along the wires, making it a guided transmission medium.

D. Coaxial cable: Has a central conductor surrounded by insulation and shielding, guiding signals along a physical path. …
qs.rel: Guided: twisted pair, coaxial, fibre. Unguided: radio, microwave, infrared, satellite, laser. Infrared is wireless even though short-range. Coaxial carries electrical signals; fibre carries light by total internal reflection.

qs.stem: Which of the following connector is used by Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP)?
qs.sol:
Concept: Physical-layer cabling standards pair a specific cable type with a specific connector shape and pin layout. For twisted-pair copper networking cable, the TIA/EIA-568 standard specifies an 8-position, 8-contact (8P8C) modular connector, popularly known as RJ45; a cable and connector are compatible only when both belong to the same standard family.

Application: Unshielded Twisted Pair (UTP) Ethernet cable is terminated at both ends with an RJ45 connector, which clips into the RJ45 port on network devices (switches, routers, NICs) and carries all eight conductors of the cable for Ethernet signaling. So, among the options given, RJ45 is the connector used with UTP cable. …
qs.rel: UTP uses RJ-45 (8 pins); telephones use RJ-11; coax uses BNC; fibre uses SC/ST/LC. Cable categories: Cat5 100 Mbps, Cat5e/6 1 Gbps, Cat6a 10 Gbps; maximum length 100 m. Straight vs crossover cables.

qs.stem: Which of the following is not an example of unguided transmission media?
qs.sol:
Unguided media = wireless (air, space)

Guided media = wired (cables)

 Coaxial cable is guided, so it is NOT unguided
qs.rel: Coaxial is guided; radio, microwave, infrared and light (laser) are unguided. Propagation modes: ground, sky, line-of-sight. Radio waves omnidirectional, microwaves unidirectional.

qs.stem: Twisted-pair cables transmit signals in the form of:
qs.sol: Twisted-pair cables consist of pairs of copper wires twisted together to reduce electromagnetic interference. These cables transmit data signals in the form of electrical currents flowing through the copper conductors. When a device sends information, it converts digital data into varying electrical voltages that travel along the wires to the receiving end. This distinguishes twisted-pair cables from fiber optic cables, which use light pulses (Options A and D), or wireless systems that transmit radio waves (Option C). Since twisted-pair cables rely on copper wiring rather than optical fibers or air-based transmission, the correct answer is Option B (Electric current). …
qs.rel: Twisted pair carries electrical current (twisting cancels interference), coax too; fibre carries light; unguided carry radio, microwave or infrared. UTP is cheaper, STP shielded; both attenuate with distance.

qs.stem: In computer networking, a Repeater is a device that operates only in the _____ layer.
qs.sol: A repeater regenerates signals and works at the Physical layer of the OSI model.
qs.rel: Repeater/hub = physical layer, regenerates signal; bridge/switch = data link; router = network; gateway = any (up to application). Hub is a multiport repeater with one collision domain, a switch has one per port.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?

(i) Fibre optics provide faster data transmission than copper wires.

(ii) Shielded twisted pair does not suffer from attenuation.
qs.sol:
Correct answer: Only (ii)

Statement (i) is TRUE: fibre optics use light signals and generally provide faster, higher-bandwidth transmission than copper wires.

Statement (ii) is FALSE: shielded twisted pair is still a physical copper medium and suffers attenuation over distance.

Shielding helps reduce electromagnetic interference, but it does not remove attenuation.
qs.rel: Fibre has higher bandwidth, lower attenuation and EMI immunity than copper; STP still suffers attenuation because it is copper (shielding reduces EMI/crosstalk, not signal loss). Fibre is costly and harder to splice.

qs.stem: A router works at the __________ layer in the OSI model and __________ layer in TCP/IP model.
qs.sol:
Concept: A router is a Layer-3 internetworking device. Its job is logical (IP) addressing and forwarding packets between different networks, so it lives at the layer responsible for end-to-end logical addressing and path selection in each reference model.

In the OSI model, logical addressing and routing of packets are handled by the Network layer (Layer 3) — this is where the router makes its forwarding decisions.

In the TCP/IP model, that same logical-addressing-and-routing responsibility belongs to the Internet layer (the home of the IP protocol), which is the TCP/IP counterpart of OSI's Network layer. …
qs.rel: Router: OSI network layer = TCP/IP internet layer. It separates broadcast domains and forwards by IP. Switch (L2) separates collision domains; layer-3 switch adds routing. Gateway converts protocols.

qs.stem: Match the following.
qs.sol:
a. Repeater  -> (iv)Works at Physical Layer

b. Bridge  ->   (iii)Works at Data Link Layer

c. Routers  ->  (i)   Works at Network Layer

d. Gateway  ->  (ii)  Works at Transport Layer (in this context)
qs.note: Table/figure from the original paper was not captured. Use the explanation to see the correct matching.
qs.rel: Device-layer match: repeater (physical), bridge (data link), router (network), gateway (higher layers; here transport). Bridge filters by MAC and separates collision domains; router also separates broadcast domains.

qs.stem: Match the following.
qs.sol:
Hub → Physical

Switch → Data Link

Router → Network

Gateway → Application
qs.note: Table/figure from the original paper was not captured. Use the explanation to see the correct matching.
qs.rel: Hub = physical, switch = data link, router = network, gateway = application (protocol conversion). Neighbouring facts: switch has MAC table, router has routing table, brouter combines both.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a propagation mode for propagating light along optical channels?
qs.sol:
A guided mode is an electromagnetic field pattern that can propagate along an optical fibre. Mode count and refractive-index profile describe different properties of the same fibre.

Single-mode and multimode classify the supported guided patterns; step-index and graded-index classify how refractive index varies across the core.

Application

Interpret the paper’s broad use of “propagation mode” as fibre transmission terminology, including both mode count and index profile.

Multimode supports several guided patterns, whereas single mode supports the fundamental spatial mode at the operating wavelength. …
qs.rel: Fibre modes: single-mode and multimode (step-index and graded-index). 'Ungraded index' is not a mode. Single-mode: laser, ~9 micron core, long distance; multimode: LED, 50/62.5 micron, short distance, modal dispersion.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement is correct regarding unguided media (wireless)?
I. Unguided media transport electromagnetic waves without using a physical conductor.
II. Unguided signals can travel from the source to destination in ground propagation way.
qs.sol: Unguided media carry electromagnetic waves without a physical conductor, and wireless signals can propagate by ground propagation, sky propagation, or line-of-sight propagation. Therefore both statements are correct.
qs.rel: Unguided media: EM waves with no conductor; propagation by ground (<2 MHz), sky (2-30 MHz) and line-of-sight (>30 MHz). Radio omnidirectional; microwave unidirectional (satellite, cellular); infrared cannot cross walls.

qs.stem: Which type of guided transmission medium is commonly categorized by RG (Radio Guide) ratings in computer networking?
qs.sol:
Correct answer: Coaxial Cable

RG stands for Radio Guide. RG numbers are used as designations for coaxial cable types, such as RG-6, RG-11, and RG-59.

Other guided media use different classifications: twisted-pair cables use category ratings like Cat5e/Cat6, and fiber-optic cables are described by fiber and optical specifications.

Modified from the official paper: The paper expands RG as “Radio Government”; the bank corrects the expansion while preserving the RG-rating question.
qs.rel: Coaxial cables are classified by RG numbers (RG-6, RG-58, RG-59) with characteristic impedance (50 or 75 ohm). Thinnet RG-58 10Base2 185 m, Thicknet 10Base5 500 m. Cat1-7 classify twisted pair; fibre by mode.

qs.stem: Which of the following with respect to a network device router is true?

opts.A: A router connects segments of a LAN.
opts.B: A router is an amplifier but not a regenerator.
opts.D: A router does not forward every frame.

qs.sol:
A router examines network-layer information and can filter traffic according to routing and policy. It is not a signal amplifier and operates on packets rather than forwarding frames as such.

A router can filter traffic using network-layer information and policy.
qs.rel: Router: layer-3 device with filtering and forwarding via routing tables; connects different networks, separates broadcast domains. It is not an amplifier (repeater) and does forward packets. Hub/bridge/switch lower layers.

qs.sol: Transmission speed in a network depends on the medium used to carry signals. Among the given options, optical fibre provides the highest transmission speed because it uses light signals, which travel at the speed of light and experience minimal signal loss over long distances. Coaxial cable and twisted pair cable use electrical signals, which are slower and more prone to interference and attenuation. Electrical cable, typically copper-based, also has lower bandwidth and higher signal degradation. Therefore, optical fibre is the best choice for high-speed data transmission. …

qs.stem: A repeater operates at __________ layer.
qs.sol:
Concept: In the OSI model, a repeater regenerates and retransmits raw signals without interpreting data, so it works at the Physical Layer.

Therefore, the answer is Physical Layer.

qs.stem: Which transmission media provides the highest transmission speed in a network?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol: Optical fiber provides the highest transmission speed in a network because it uses light signals to transmit data. This allows for very high bandwidth and minimal signal loss over long distances. Unlike copper cables (coaxial and twisted-pair), optical fiber is immune to electromagnetic interference and supports faster data rates, making it the best choice for high-speed networks. …

qs.stem: Fibre optics is an example of ....... .
qs.sol:
Explanation

Fibre optics is a technology that uses thin strands of glass or plastic to transmit data as light signals. Because these signals travel through a physical cable that guides them from one point to another, it is classified as guided media.
